abdicate: To give up your throne on purpose. A king or emperor who abdicates stops ruling while still alive.
abolish: To officially put an end to a law, a custom or a system. For example, abolishing the death penalty means it can no longer be used.
absolute monarch: A king or queen who holds all the power alone: they make the laws, command the army and have the last word in justice, without having to ask anyone.
amphitheatre: A huge oval arena surrounded by rows of stone seats. The Romans watched gladiator fights and animal shows there. You can still see them in Nîmes and Arles.
aqueduct: A channel built by the Romans to bring fresh water from far away into towns. Sometimes it crossed valleys on high bridges, like the Pont du Gard.
archer: A soldier who fights with a bow and arrows. English archers, with their long bows, could shoot very far and very fast.
armistice: An agreement to stop fighting in a war. It is not yet peace, but the guns fall silent.
astronaut: A person trained to travel into space in a spacecraft. In France, people sometimes say "spationaute".
barricade: A wall hastily built across a street with paving stones, carts, furniture or cars, to block soldiers or the police during an uprising.
bath: The Romans' public baths were like big swimming pools and spas, with hot, warm and cold pools. People went there to wash, relax and meet friends.
camera obscura: Latin for "dark room": a closed box or room with a tiny hole. Light coming through the hole projects an upside-down image of the outside onto the opposite wall.
cardinal: One of the highest leaders of the Catholic Church, just below the Pope. Cardinals wear red and elect the new Pope.
catholic: A Christian who belongs to the Catholic Church, led by the Pope in Rome. For centuries, most French people were Catholics.
cauldron: A large bowl in which the Olympic flame burns for the whole length of the Games.
celt: The Celts were a group of peoples who lived in much of Europe more than 2,000 years ago, from Ireland to Central Europe. The Gauls were Celts.
certificat d'études: The exam at the end of primary school in France, from 1880 to 1989. Passing it was a great source of pride for the whole family.
chemical element: One of the basic substances that everything is made of, like oxygen, iron or gold. Each one is made of one kind of atom. Scientists know about 118 of them.
cholera: A serious disease caught from dirty water. It causes terrible diarrhoea and can kill in a few days. It spread easily in cities without clean water or sewers.
châteaux of the loire: A group of magnificent castles built along the river Loire and its tributaries, mostly during the Renaissance, such as Chambord, Chenonceau, Blois and Amboise.
cinématographe: The machine invented by the Lumière brothers in 1895. It could film, develop and project moving pictures onto a screen. The word "cinema" comes from it!
civil registration: The official recording of births, marriages and deaths. It proves who you are, when and where you were born, and who your parents are.
climate change: The warming of the Earth caused mostly by the gases released when we burn oil, gas and coal. It brings more heatwaves, droughts, storms and floods.
collaborate: During the Second World War, to collaborate meant to help the German occupiers, for example by working with them or handing over people they were hunting.
colonisation: When a country takes control of a territory far away, rules its people and uses its riches. The territory becomes a colony.
constitution: The most important law of a country. It says how the country is governed, who holds power, and what rights the citizens have.
constitutional monarchy: A country with a king or queen who must obey a constitution and share power with an elected parliament.
count: In the Middle Ages, a lord who governed a region, called a county, in the name of the king or the emperor.
coup d'état: When someone seizes power by force or by surprise, without an election, usually with the help of the army.
craftspeople: Skilled workers who make things with their hands, such as stonemasons, carpenters, glassmakers or blacksmiths.
crusades: Wars led by Christians of Europe in the Middle Ages to take control of Jerusalem and the Holy Land. They lasted about 200 years and caused many deaths on all sides.
daguerreotype: The first photographic process sold to the public, invented by Louis Daguerre in 1839. Each picture was unique, on a shiny silver-coated plate.
dauphin: The title of the eldest son of the King of France, the heir to the throne. It means "dolphin", which was on the coat of arms of the region of Dauphiné.
decimal: Counting in groups of 10. In the metric system, each unit is 10 times bigger or smaller than the next, which makes calculations easy.
dictionary: A book that lists the words of a language in alphabetical order and explains their meaning and spelling.
diversity: Variety. A diverse society is made up of people of different origins, cultures, religions and ways of life.
druid: A priest of the Gauls. Druids were also scholars, judges and teachers. They knew the stars and plants, and they learned everything by heart without writing it down.
duel: A fight between two people, often with swords or pistols, to settle a question of honour. Many nobles died in duels, and the king forbade them.
embroidery: Decoration made by sewing coloured threads onto a fabric with a needle, stitch by stitch.
emperor: A ruler of an empire, a very large state often made up of many peoples and regions. It is a title even higher than king.
estates-general: A great assembly of representatives of the three orders of French society: the clergy, the nobility and the Third Estate. The king called it only in times of crisis.
etiquette: The strict rules of behaviour at the king's court: how to greet, where to stand, who may sit, and even who hands the king his shirt!
fascism: A political system created by Mussolini in Italy. A leader holds all the power, freedoms are removed, opponents are persecuted and violence and war are glorified.
feudalism: The system of the Middle Ages: a lord gave land to a vassal, who swore to be loyal and to fight for him. Peasants worked the land and received protection.
francophonie: All the people and countries in the world that speak French. An international organisation brings together about 90 states and governments.
frank: The Franks were a Germanic people who settled in Gaul at the end of the Roman Empire. They gave their name to France.
freedom: Being free to think, speak, move and live as you wish, as long as you respect the law and the freedom of others.
freedom of conscience: The right to believe in the religion you choose, to change religion, or to have no religion at all.
gallo-roman: The mixed civilisation of Gaul under Roman rule: Gauls who adopted the Roman language, laws, towns and way of life, while keeping some of their own traditions.
gaul: The Gauls were the Celtic peoples who lived in Gaul, roughly today's France, Belgium and Switzerland, before the Roman conquest.
gothic: A style of architecture that appeared in France in the 12th century, with pointed arches, very high vaults and huge stained-glass windows full of light.
guillotine: A machine with a heavy sloping blade used to execute people by cutting off their head. It was used in France from 1792 until 1977.
hand axe: A stone tool shaped like a big almond, cut on both sides to make sharp edges. Prehistoric people used it to cut, scrape and chop.
heretic: A person accused by the Church of believing ideas that go against its official teaching. In the Middle Ages, heretics could be burned.
holocaust: The murder of about six million Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators during the Second World War. It is also called the Shoah.
homo erectus: An ancient human species that appeared in Africa almost 2 million years ago. It walked upright, made stone tools and was the first to leave Africa.
homo sapiens: Our own species! Homo sapiens appeared in Africa about 300,000 years ago and spread across the whole world.
hunter-gatherer: A person who lives by hunting animals, fishing and gathering wild plants, fruits and roots, moving around instead of farming.
ice age: A long period when the Earth was much colder than today. Huge sheets of ice covered the north of Europe, and reindeer and mammoths lived in France.
independence: When a country becomes free to govern itself, and no longer depends on another country.
julius caesar: A famous Roman general and politician. He conquered Gaul between 58 and 51 BC, and later became the master of Rome. He was assassinated in 44 BC.
knight: A noble warrior on horseback, protected by armour. Knights had to be brave, loyal and protect the weak, according to the rules of chivalry.
laïcité: The French word for secularism: the state is neutral towards religions, favours none, and guarantees everyone the freedom to believe or not to believe.
latin: The language of the ancient Romans. French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian all come from Latin.
lycée: A secondary school for pupils aged about 15 to 18. The lycées were created by Napoleon in 1802.
maastricht treaty: A treaty signed in 1992 in Maastricht, in the Netherlands, that created the European Union and planned a common currency, the euro.
megalith: A huge standing stone, or a group of huge stones, raised by prehistoric people, like the menhirs and dolmens of Carnac.
merovingian: The first dynasty of Frankish kings, from Clovis to the 8th century. It was named after Merovech, Clovis's grandfather.
metre: The basic unit of length in the metric system. It was first defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the Equator.
microbe: A living thing so small that it can only be seen with a microscope. Some microbes cause diseases, but many are useful, like those that make yoghurt.
mobilised: Called up to join the army because of a war. In 1914, millions of French men were mobilised.
neanderthal: A human species that lived in Europe and Asia from about 400,000 to 40,000 years ago. Neanderthals were strong, made tools and buried their dead.
neolithic: The "New Stone Age", when people began to farm, raise animals, live in villages and make pottery. In France, it began about 7,000 years ago.
nobel prize: A very famous international prize given every year since 1901 to people who have done great work in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, peace and economics.
oath: A solemn promise, often made in front of witnesses or on something sacred.
occitan: A regional language of the south of France, spoken in the Middle Ages by troubadours. It is still spoken and taught today.
old french: The French language of the Middle Ages, which came from Latin. It is quite different from modern French: you would find it hard to understand!
olympic games: The world's greatest sports competition, held every four years, where athletes from almost every country compete. It was inspired by the Games of ancient Greece.
orbit: The path a satellite, a planet or a moon follows as it goes round another object in space, again and again.
ordinance: A law made by the king, in the time of the monarchy.
overseas territories: The parts of France located far from Europe: Guadeloupe, Martinique, French Guiana, Réunion, Mayotte, New Caledonia, French Polynesia, and others.
paid holiday: Days off during which workers still receive their wages. In France, they were first given in 1936.
paralympic game: The Paralympic Games are a major sports competition for athletes with disabilities, held just after the Olympic Games, in the same city.
paratrooper: A soldier who jumps from a plane with a parachute to land behind the enemy's lines.
parliament: An assembly of representatives elected by the citizens, who vote the laws. In France, the Parliament is made up of the National Assembly and the Senate.
pasteurisation: Heating a food such as milk or fruit juice, then cooling it quickly, to kill harmful microbes. It was invented by Louis Pasteur.
philosopher: A person who thinks deeply about big questions: what is true, what is just, how should we live? In the 18th century, the philosophers wanted to use reason to improve society.
photographic plate: A plate of glass or metal covered with a substance that changes when light hits it. It was used to take photos before film and digital cameras.
pigment: A coloured powder, taken from earth, minerals or plants, used to make paint. Prehistoric artists used red and yellow ochre and black charcoal.
plague: A very dangerous disease carried by fleas that live on rats. In the Middle Ages, the Black Death killed about a third of Europe's population.
prefect: A high official appointed by the government to represent the state in a department. The prefect of the Seine was in charge of Paris.
privilege: A special right or advantage that only some people have. Before 1789, nobles and clergy had privileges, such as paying fewer taxes.
protestant: A Christian who follows the Reformation, started in the 16th century by Luther and Calvin, who broke away from the Pope's authority.
racism: The false and harmful idea that some human groups are superior to others because of their skin colour or origin. All human beings are equal.
radio: A way of sending sounds far away without wires, using invisible waves. At first, it sent Morse code; later, voices and music.
radioactivity: The ability of some materials, like uranium or radium, to give off invisible rays and energy. These rays can be useful, but also dangerous.
reason: Our ability to think, to reflect logically and to understand things by ourselves, by looking for proof.
referendum: A vote in which all citizens answer "yes" or "no" to a question, such as whether to adopt a new constitution.
relic: An object that belonged to a saint or to Jesus, or a part of a saint's body, kept and honoured by believers.
religious tolerance: Accepting that other people have a different religion, or none, and letting them practise it in peace.
renaissance: Meaning "rebirth": a period of the 15th and 16th centuries when artists and scholars in Europe rediscovered ancient Greece and Rome and created wonderful new works.
republic: A country where power does not belong to a king but to the people, who elect their leaders for a limited time.
resistance: The men and women who secretly fought against the German occupation and the Vichy regime during the Second World War.
retreat: When an army moves back, away from the enemy, because it cannot continue to advance or fight.
right to vote: The right to choose your representatives and give your opinion in elections. In France, women obtained it in 1944.
rivet: A metal pin, heated until red-hot, then hammered to hold two metal plates firmly together.
rocket: A vehicle propelled by powerful engines that burn fuel and push gas downwards, strong enough to leave the Earth and go into space.
rose window: A large round stained-glass window, shaped like a flower, found in Gothic cathedrals.
schengen area: A group of European countries where people can cross borders without showing a passport. It is named after a village in Luxembourg.
secular: Not linked to any religion. A secular school does not teach any religion, so that all children can be welcome there, whatever their beliefs.
separation of powers: The idea that the power to make laws, the power to govern and the power to judge must be held by different people, so that nobody becomes a tyrant.
sewer: An underground pipe or tunnel that carries dirty water away from homes and streets.
slave trade: The capture and sale of people from Africa, who were transported across the Atlantic Ocean in slave ships and sold as slaves in the Americas.
slavery: A terrible system in which people are treated as property. Enslaved people were bought and sold, forced to work without pay and had no freedom.
social security: A system created in France in 1945: everyone pays a little money each month, so that everyone can be cared for when ill and receive help in old age.
st bartholomew's day massacre: The massacre of thousands of Protestants by Catholics, which began in Paris on the 24th of August 1572, Saint Bartholomew's Day.
stained glass: Pieces of coloured glass held together by lead strips to make pictures in windows. When light shines through, the colours glow.
strike: When workers stop working together to demand better wages or working conditions.
supersonic: Faster than the speed of sound, which is about 1,200 km/h. A supersonic plane creates a loud "boom".
trade union: An organisation of workers that defends their rights and interests, for example their wages and working conditions.
trench: A long, deep ditch dug in the ground where soldiers sheltered from enemy bullets and shells, especially during the First World War.
triangulation: A method of measuring long distances by measuring the angles of a chain of triangles between high points, like towers and hills.
unesco world heritage: A list of the most precious places on Earth, chosen by UNESCO, an organisation of the United Nations, so that they are protected for future generations.
universal suffrage: The right for all adult citizens to vote. In France, men obtained it in 1848, and women in 1944.
vaccine: A medicine that teaches the body to defend itself against a disease, often by giving it a weakened or dead microbe, so that it will not get sick later.
viking: The Vikings were sailors and warriors from Scandinavia who raided the coasts of Europe in their long ships from the 8th to the 11th century.
war memorial: A monument, in almost every French town and village, bearing the names of the local people who died in wars.
world cup: The biggest football competition in the world, held every four years, in which national teams compete to become world champion.
world's fair: A huge international exhibition where countries show off their inventions, products and cultures. In French, it is called an "Exposition universelle".
